The real story: Fish farm staff found a dead orca drifting in Kåfjorden, North Troms, Norway, on February 10, 2026. Whale researcher Eve Jourdain said it was the first time an orca had been documented in Norway to die after a collision with a vessel. Source: NRK, published February 17, 2026.

Most whales that die at sea sink to the bottom and are never found. This one drifted into view. On February 10, 2026, employees at a fish farm in Kåfjorden, in the far north of Norway, spotted a dead orca floating in the fjord and raised the alarm.

Whale researcher Eve Jourdain of the University of Oslo, who also works with the Norwegian Orca Survey, examined the case and described it as unique: for the first time in Norway, an orca has been documented to have died after being struck by a vessel. Professor Audun Rikardsen of the Arctic University of Norway, who alerted her, agreed the find was important. He thinks it unlikely that a tourist boat was responsible, and because the whale was found in Kåfjorden, he believes it probably died not far from where it was found.

The significance goes beyond one animal. Norway's orcas follow herring along the northern coast each winter, in waters busy with fishing boats and traffic, yet until now there were no concrete signs that shipping could kill one. Jourdain said she herself had not realized it was such a real threat. A single carcass turned up by chance, and it changed what researchers know is possible.

Rocky, a 29 year old bottlenose dolphin, has died at Selwo Marina in Spain, according to the marine park’s announcement.

Born at Zoo Madrid on March 13, 1997, Rocky spent his life moving between several facilities. His recorded history includes Aquópolis, Oceanogràfic in Valencia, and Marineland Antibes in France, where he lived for many years.

In July, Rocky was transferred from Marineland Antibes to Selwo Marina. His death came only a few months after that move.

Selwo Marina said its team was deeply saddened by the loss and that a post mortem examination was underway to determine the cause of death. The park did not announce a cause in the statement provided.

Rocky’s story is a reminder of the many changes captive dolphins can experience throughout their lives. For now, the cause of his death remains unconfirmed, and it is important not to assume that his recent transfer was responsible.
Rest in peace, Rocky. 💙

🐋 HOW MANY BELUGA WHALES ARE LIVING IN CAPTIVITY AROUND THE WORLD?

According to Ceta Base, a global database that tracks whales and dolphins in human care, 165 beluga whales were listed as living in captivity worldwide as of October 6, 2026. They were recorded across 42 facilities in 10 countries. citeturn614462search0

The database lists facilities in Russia, China, the United States, Japan, South Korea, Turkey, Iceland, Spain, Taiwan, and Ukraine.

Of those 165 belugas, 112 were wild caught, 52 were born in human care, and one was rescued. That means roughly two thirds of the listed animals originally came from the wild. citeturn614462search0

Belugas are highly social Arctic whales known for their white bodies, expressive faces, and wide range of vocalizations. In the wild, they travel, communicate, and navigate through changing Arctic environments.

These numbers can change as whales are born, die, or move between facilities, so the total is a dated estimate rather than a permanent count.

What do you think? Should belugas continue to be kept in aquariums, or should the world work toward ending their captivity?

A new step toward protection could make a difference for one of the most endangered orca populations in the world. 💙

The Southern Resident killer whales, known for their close family bonds and distinctive J, K, and L pods, face serious challenges to their survival. Their population depends heavily on Chinook salmon, an important food source that has declined in many parts of the whales’ range.

California is an important part of this story because these orcas also use waters along the state’s coast. A potential listing under the California Endangered Species Act could provide an additional layer of protection alongside existing federal safeguards.

However, advancing a petition is not the same as granting endangered status. The next steps in the review process will help determine what protections may follow.

Protecting these whales also means protecting the salmon and healthy marine ecosystems they depend on. Every step toward understanding and addressing these challenges matters.

The real story: A study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, led by Dr. Éadin O'Mahony of the University of St Andrews and reported January 22, 2026, found that bubble-net feeding is spreading among humpback whales in the Kitimat Fjord System of northern British Columbia, in Gitga'at First Nation territory. The researchers think the technique may have been introduced by whales arriving from other areas such as Alaska. Source: Discover Wildlife (BBC Wildlife), published January 22, 2026.

Bubble-net feeding is one of the most spectacular things an animal does. Humpback whales dive beneath a school of fish, swim in a spiral while blowing a curtain of bubbles, then surge up through the middle with their mouths open. It is cooperative, it is coordinated, and many scientists see it as a form of tool use. For years, tourists have flocked to Alaska to watch it.

Now researchers say it is showing up where it used to be rare. A study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, carried out in the Kitimat Fjord System of northern British Columbia, in the territory of the Gitga'at First Nation, found bubble-net feeding spreading through the local humpback population. Drone footage from the North Coast Cetacean Society captured whales bubble-netting off Fin Island. The team's leading explanation is that immigrant whales have arrived in the area and brought the strategy with them, teaching it to whales who didn't know how.

That makes this a story about culture, not just feeding. Lead author Dr. Éadin O'Mahony says it matters especially as whales recover from the whaling era: "Cultural loss can be just as damaging as population loss." Skills like this one are learned from other whales, which means that losing the animals who hold them can erase knowledge as well as numbers, and protecting the places where distinct behaviors are concentrated could help protect the behaviors themselves. A hunting technique is spreading through a whale community the way a fashion spreads through a town, and scientists are watching it happen.
